name: Brick
seoDesc: Brick: work out bricks needed from the wall length and the wall area. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: bricks needed is what the Brick calculator works out, and it gets there from the wall length, the wall area, the brick length and the brick height. That makes it useful for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Brick calculator work?
sections.html:
The Brick calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports bricks needed in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of wall and the mortar ratio); then you type in the wall length (L), the wall area, the brick length (l) and the brick height (h).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Brick calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Bricks needed=rounded up, (wall area × type of wall ÷ (brick height (h) × brick length (l) + brick height (h) × mortar joint thickness (t) + brick length (l) × mortar joint thickness (t) + (mortar joint thickness (t) ^ 2)))
Total bricks needed=rounded up, ((1 ÷ 100) × (brick wastage + 100) × rounded up, (wall area × type of wall ÷ (brick height (h) × brick length (l) + brick height (h) × mortar joint thickness (t) + brick length (l) × mortar joint thickness (t) + (mortar joint thickness (t) ^ 2))))
Wall height (H)=wall area ÷ wall length (L)
Cost of bricks=(price per brick × rounded up, ((1 ÷ 100) × (brick wastage + 100) × rounded up, (wall area × type of wall ÷ (brick height (h) × brick length (l) + brick height (h) × mortar joint thickness (t) + brick length (l) × mortar joint thickness (t) + (mortar joint thickness (t) ^ 2)))))
Mortar joint thickness (t)=(1 ÷ 2) × (the square root of ((brick width (w) × wall area × type of wall − wet volume) × ((brick height (h) ^ 2) × brick width (w) × wall area × type of wall − (brick height (h) ^ 2) × wet volume + 2 × brick height (h) × brick length (l) × brick width (w) × wall area × type of wall + 2 × brick height (h) × brick length (l) × wet volume + (brick length (l) ^ 2) × brick width (w) × wall area × type of wall − (brick length (l) ^ 2) × wet volume)) − (brick height (h) + brick length (l)) × (brick width (w) × wall area × type of wall − wet volume)) ÷ (brick width (w) × wall area × type of wall − wet volume)
Dry volume to wet volume ratio=dry volume ÷ wet volume

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in meters

  • Length, opening in millimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Brick calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the wall length, the wall area and the brick length — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Brick calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns bricks needed, derived from the wall length, the wall area and the brick length. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Brick calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the wall length, the wall area, the brick length and the brick height, which is 18 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter wall length (L) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Wall length (L) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Brick calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
